trans.sense: relaxing of tension, especially between countries; an instance of this

examples.text: They had a vague feeling that after the dislocations and the violence which the Impressionists inflicted on the picturesque, the eyes of their contemporaries necessarily needed a little rest. Instinct and reflection were no less ready to warn them that the last hours were at hand of one of those reactions, or, to speak more accurately, those détentes, which are so frequent in the history of art.
examples.ref: 1897 May 15, André Michel, “The Salons at Paris”, in The Athenæum: Journal of English and Foreign Literature, Science, the Fine Arts, Music and the Drama, number 3629, London: Printed by John Edward Francis, […]; published […], by John C. Francis, →OCLC, pages 656–657:

examples.text: Although the Pope [Leo XIII]'s decision was in favour of Spain, it brought about quite a détente between Berlin and Rome.
examples.ref: 1899, Julien de Narfon, “A Political Pope”, in G. A. Raper, transl., Pope Leo XIII: His Life and Work […], London: Chapman & Hall, →OCLC, page 185:

examples.text: This intellectual and moral unrest is the inner reason for the continued talk on triple alliances, dual alliances, ententes and detentes. Monarchs and statesmen always seem engaged in maneuvers on the diplomatic chessboard, in order to isolate one Power and to combine others.

examples.text: The receipt of the letter brought about a considerable détente; and the Lebanese were prevailed upon to send the President's Chef de Cabinet to meet General [Paul] Beynet on his arrival at the airport.
